newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Mediametrie defends TV viewing figures.
newsitem.headline: French Mediametrie defends TV viewing figures.

text.p: Jacqueline Aglietta, chairman of French audience measurement body Mediametrie, on Friday defended TV viewing figures published by Mediametrie.
Mediametrie's figures have recently come under fire in a debate on audience numbers, which is now widening to include the content of French TV programmes.

"Audience measurement tools are made by and for the profession, and you cannot appropriate them in a partisan fashion," she said in an interview published in Friday's issue of afternoon newspaper Le Monde.

"Mediametrie has a difficult role, that of taking the temperature. If you are not satisfied with the results from the thermometer, you may be tempted to break it, but that is not the answer," she said.
Aglietta said Mediametrie was owned by television stations, advertising agencies, advertisers and radio stations, which guaranteed its impartiality.
She did not comment directly on a debate raging in France over whether over a million French television viewers stopped watching TV in the first quarter of this year.

On Tuesday advertising space specialist Carat's measurement arm reopened the debate, issuing a statement saying there was a fall of at least 1.3 million viewers in France between February 3 and April 20, compared to the same period of 1996.
Last week Mediametrie, referring to earlier French newspaper reports of such a slide, denied that the TV audience had in fact shrivelled.
More people watched television at least once a day in France in the first quarter, but they switched on for less time, Mediametrie said.
Carat, however, challenged the basis of its figures, saying it only counted viewers as people who switched on for at least a minute.

"It is not up to television or radio stations or advertising agencies to decide themselves the standards for qualifying the audience. Anyone can use as they wish the 150,000 pieces of information that Mediametrie analyses each day, but the communication of this data should be organised," Aglietta said.
The debate is starting to shift from being purely a numbers game to looking to what is on television as an explanation.

Le Monde on Friday reported that polling institute BVA found over half those surveyed in a poll conducted late last month were satisfied by television programmes broadcast by both French public and private television stations.

The poll, carried out for advertising agency 3B for the 20th international conference of public television stations, which opens in Nantes on Sunday, found 52 percent of those surveyed were happy with programmes on public television channels, while 54 percent were satisfied with programmes on private channels.
Daily newspaper Le Figaro this week said there was a move away from general, terrestrial channels to thematic channels carried on the newer cable and satellite services.
An editorial comment in women's weekly Elle this week said people were fed up with boring programmes and preferred to do other things besides sit in front of the television.
